tasks.title: Orientation
tasks.goal: get your bearings before anything is asked of you.
tasks.instructions: With score open at State 0, set the right panel to State 1 (`mem2reg`). Select `return weighted + wasted;` in the C source and follow its highlight into IR. Change the right panel to CFG and select a block; inspect its links back to IR instructions and C lines. There is nothing to submit.

tasks.title: What changed?
tasks.goal: work out what the optimiser did to a program overall, before worrying about how it did it.
tasks.instructions: Compare score at State 0 (unoptimised) and State 12 (`final_cleanup`) in IR. State 13 (`-O3`) was compiled separately. Name two changes you can see. You may use the source and explanations. A brief or partial answer is fine.

tasks.title: Which pass did it?
tasks.goal: trace a specific change back to the pass responsible for it.

tasks.title: Following source into the graph
tasks.goal: locate a C condition in IR and interpret its control-flow graph block.
tasks.instructions: In binary_search, set both panels to State 3 (`simplifycfg`), with IR left and CFG right. Select `while (lo < hi)` in C, follow the highlight to its IR comparison, then identify that instruction’s block and its outgoing arrows.

tasks.title: A change in the shape of the program
tasks.goal: notice a structural change, not just a textual one.
tasks.instructions: In binary_search, compare CFG at State 6 (`loop_canonical`) and State 7 (`loop_rotate`). Describe a branch or loop-path change, using a block or arrow, and say what you think it does. You may inspect IR too.

tasks.title: What does this correspondence tell you?
tasks.goal: interpret a recorded correspondence and the confidence attached to it.
tasks.instructions: In quick_sort, set the left panel to State 8 (`licm`) and the right to State 9 (`indvars`), with IR in both. Choose `partition`. Select `if (a[j] <= pivot)` in C, then select the highlighted right-panel getelementptr for `a[j]`. What relationship does the tool show, and what confidence wording appears beside the link? What does the optimisation explanation say happened? Keep the link’s confidence separate from the explanation’s qualification.

tasks.instructions: Explore for about five minutes. Investigate something that interests you and describe what you found.

taskIntroduction: Three small C programs are already loaded. You do not need to write or compile code.

Each program has fourteen recorded states: State 0 is the unoptimised baseline compiled with -O0; States 1–12 are produced by successive compiler passes applied to the preceding output; State 13 is compiled separately with -O3.

T0 is the orientation; the six tasks are T1–T6. T1–T5 open on the named example at State 0 with IR in both panels; set the states and views named in each task. T6 continues with T5’s example, states, function, and views, with the previous selection cleared; continue there or change them. You can use the C source, highlighting, explanations, and word help. This study evaluates the tool, not you; the tasks are not an unaided test. Answer at your own level of detail: brief, partial, or blank answers are useful. You may also skip or choose “I could not work this out”.

As you move between sections and tasks, your answers remain a draft in this browser tab; navigation does not submit them. Continuing locks that task’s answers. Duration is recorded from task presentation and includes visible reading, setup, exploration, and answering. Paused time, hidden-tab time, and reload downtime are excluded. There is no time limit.

blocks.text: Understanding what compilers do to your code
Thanks for taking a look. This is a research study for an undergraduate thesis at the University of Queensland.

When you compile a C program, the compiler does not just translate it — it rewrites it. It deletes work it can prove is pointless, moves calculations out of loops, merges and splits branches, and reshapes the control flow, all before a single instruction of machine code is produced. Most of that happens where nobody can see it. You write the source, you get a binary, and the interesting part in between is invisible.

irexplorer is a web tool that makes that middle part visible. It takes a small C program, compiles it with LLVM one optimisation pass at a time, and lets you look at the program's intermediate representation — the internal form the compiler actually works on — at each step along the way. You can put any two of those steps side by side, read the textual form and the control-flow graph together, and see what a given pass changed.

This study evaluates how useful irexplorer is when students and non-expert developers use it to explore compiler changes. The tasks give you questions to try with the tool; they are not an unaided test of what you already know or an assessment of you. You can use the tool's views and explanations, and answer at your own level of detail.

You do not need to know anything about compilers to take part. Being able to read basic C is enough. If you have never seen LLVM intermediate representation before, you are exactly the person this study needs.
The Continue button is at the bottom of this page. Scroll down and select it when you are ready.
About 35 minutes, done in your own time, in a browser.

items: A few questions about your background (about 4 minutes) — what you have studied and how familiar you are with the topics involved. This is so I can describe who took part; there are no right answers.

Six short tasks using the tool (about 20 minutes) — each one gives you a goal, such as working out what changed between two versions of a program. Some have a correct answer and some are open-ended. You are welcome to say you could not work something out; that is a useful result and it is the tool being tested, not you.
A closing survey (about 8 minutes) — rating statements about the tool and writing whatever you want to say about it in your own words.
